h1: Non-alcoholic beer styles explained: from lager to IPA
title: Non-alcoholic beer styles explained | Craft Beer School
desc: From lager to IPA and stout: how non-alcoholic beers are made, what each style tastes like and how to choose one you will enjoy.
teaser: Non-alcoholic beer now covers lager, wheat, pale ale, IPA and stout. Here is what to expect from each.
standfirst: Good non-alcoholic beer is no longer a single sweet, thin lager. The range is wide. So are the methods. This guide explains the styles and the technology behind them.
sections:
Terms differ by country, which causes real confusion. In the United Kingdom, for example, alcohol-free beer is up to 0.05% ABV and de-alcoholised beer up to 0.5%. In the United States, a beer labelled non-alcoholic must contain less than 0.5% ABV. Other countries set their own limits. Some use 0.0% as the only acceptable claim.

Check the label and the local rules. Where alcohol is restricted or banned, local law comes first and non-alcoholic products may still be regulated.

Limited fermentation. The brewer stops fermentation early or uses a special yeast that cannot ferment maltose, so little alcohol forms. Without ethanol, the beer can taste of unfermented wort: sweet, grainy, sometimes close to bread dough.

Dealcoholisation. The brewer makes a normal beer then removes the alcohol, either by vacuum distillation at low temperature or by membrane filtration. Both need specialist equipment. Some flavour goes with the alcohol. Brewers often add aroma back or blend with fresh wort.

Brewing for low alcohol. Recipe design with lower fermentable sugar and carefully chosen yeast helps beer taste complete without ethanol. Our guide for breweries covers the practical choices.

Each route has a trade-off. Limited fermentation is simple and cheap but risks a worty taste. Dealcoholisation keeps the beer's character but needs costly kit or a contract partner. Careful recipe design sits between the two and rewards a skilled brewer.

Packaging matters too. Non-alcoholic beer has no ethanol to hold back microbes and often retains some sugar, so it is usually pasteurised or sterile filtered. That is why quality control around hygiene is stricter than for regular beer.

This is the easiest style to do well. Light, crisp and refreshing, a non-alcoholic lager has little to hide and little to lose. Good ones taste of fresh bread crust with a gentle bitterness. Poor ones taste of wort or cooked vegetables. Serve at 3 to 5 °C.

The honest weakness of any non-alcoholic lager is body. Alcohol adds a sense of weight and a gentle warmth. Without it the beer can seem watery. Brewers compensate with malt choice, a little residual sugar and higher carbonation. Taste a few brands side by side and you will find big differences.

Wheat styles work well because yeast character (clove and banana in a hefeweizen, citrus and coriander in a witbier) is strong and does not depend on alcohol. Soft body and high carbonation also help non-alcoholic wheat beers feel full.

Hops carry aroma, so hoppy non-alcoholic beers can taste remarkably like the real thing. The challenge is body: alcohol adds weight and warmth. Without it a hoppy beer can feel thin and sharp. Brewers add body with oats, wheat or dextrins and dry hop generously. Bitterness feels stronger without alcohol's softness, so low-bitterness IPAs often taste more balanced.

Roasted malt gives a drink coffee and cocoa notes, which do not depend on alcohol. This is why dark non-alcoholic beers often impress people. Body and roast must be balanced, or the beer turns acrid. A little lactose or oat helps with creaminess.

Tasting notes for non-alcoholic stout often use words like espresso, dark chocolate and toast. Roast flavours are strong, so those notes are easy to pick out. This makes dark styles a good place to practise your tasting.

Acidity works without alcohol, so non-alcoholic sours are growing in range. Fruit, spice and botanical additions can fill out flavour. Compare with other style families in our beginner's map of world beer styles.

Buy a style you already like and try it cold from a clean glass. Judge aroma first, then sweetness, then bitterness, then finish. If it tastes of wort, try a different brand or method. Our how to taste beer guide helps you describe what you find.

It also helps to compare across methods. Try a limited-fermentation lager and a dealcoholised lager from different brewers on the same evening. Write down differences in sweetness, bitterness and aroma. After two or three of these comparisons you will know quickly which kind you prefer. Remember that taste is personal. The best non-alcoholic beer is the one you will happily finish.
faqs: Is non-alcoholic beer completely alcohol free?
Not always. Many beers labelled non-alcoholic contain up to 0.5% ABV. Only those labelled 0.0% aim for none. Rules differ by country.
By limiting fermentation or by removing alcohol from finished beer with vacuum distillation or membranes. Careful recipe and yeast choice also help.
Why do some taste like wort?
Beers that skip full fermentation keep sweet, grainy compounds that fermentation normally removes. Dealcoholised beer and well designed recipes avoid this.
Which style is the best start?
A non-alcoholic lager or wheat beer, served cold. They are the most forgiving styles.
